opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the key takeaway is that the "emergence" story people were telling is, to a large extent, a story about how we measure, not about some sudden qualitative change inside the model.

When we wrote down the simple model, assuming per-token error falls off smoothly, roughly as a power law in scale, and then asked what happens when you score with something harsh like exact match or multiple-choice accuracy, the math says you should see exactly those sharp, unpredictable-looking jumps. If you need every token in a long answer to be right, a smooth improvement in per-token probability gets raised to a big power, and it looks flat for a long time and then shoots up. Score the same outputs with a continuous metric, like token edit distance or Brier score, and the prediction is that the curve becomes smooth and predictable.

What was satisfying was that real models largely behaved the way the toy model said. When we took the same model families and tasks and switched to continuous metrics, a lot of the dramatic emergence just went away, and you saw steady, fairly predictable improvement. We could also go the other direction, taking vision models where nobody claimed emergence and inducing "emergent" curves just by picking a discontinuous metric.

The broader lesson, and what I hope people take from it, is twofold. First, be careful about which metric you report and what it implies, because metric choice can manufacture or hide phenomena. Second, there's good news for safety and planning: if a lot of capability growth is smoother than it looks, it may be more forecastable than we feared. That doesn't mean nothing surprising ever happens with scale, and we were careful not to claim that. But the burden of proof has shifted. Before calling something emergent, you should check whether it survives a change of metric and enough evaluation data.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the key takeaway for me is that the theory and the empirical behavior actually line up a lot better than I expected going in, and the places where they diverge are informative rather than embarrassing.

So just to set the stage, the thing we were doing in the paper was trying to explain emergent abilities, these claims that models suddenly acquire capabilities at some scale, and our argument was that a lot of that is an artifact of the metric you choose. If you measure with something discontinuous, like exact match accuracy, where you get zero credit unless every token is right, then smooth improvements in per-token likelihood get transformed into something that looks like a step function. And you can write that down. You can take a model whose per-token error decreases smoothly and predictably with scale, apply the nonlinear metric, and derive what the curve should look like.

And when we overlaid those predicted curves on actual model families, GPT-3, the open models we had access to at the time, the shape matched. You see the flat region, you see the sharp rise, and it shows up at roughly the scale the theory says it should, given the sequence length and the underlying per-token trend. That was the satisfying part, because it meant the "emergence" was explainable from quantities you could measure on much smaller models. You didn't need to invoke anything mysterious.

But I want to be careful about what that does and doesn't say. The theory is a sufficiency argument. It says this mechanism is enough to produce curves that look like this. It doesn't say nothing else is going on. And in practice, there were cases where the fit was looser, where the real curve rose earlier or more gradually than the pure prediction, and I think that's where the interesting science is. That gap is telling you about things the simple model doesn't capture, maybe data composition, maybe genuine representational changes, maybe just noise from how the benchmark was constructed.

So the takeaway I'd give people is twofold. One, before you claim a capability is emergent, check whether a smooth metric on the same model tells a different story, because often it does. And two, treat the theoretical curve as a baseline, a null hypothesis. Deviations from it are where you should be looking, not the sharp jump itself.

r001.rationale: The response says the theory and empirical behavior line up well and that predicted curve shapes matched those observed across model families.

astra-6.text: I think the key takeaway is that the theory gives us a useful way to understand the behavior, but we have to distinguish predicting a trend from predicting exactly what a real model will do. If the curves line up, that’s evidence that the theory is capturing something meaningful. Where they diverge is also interesting, because that tells us where our assumptions may be missing something. So I’d treat that comparison as a way to understand both the explanatory power of the theory and its limits.
